title: Motility, Digestion, and Absorption
subject: Gastrointestinal System (GAST)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter follows a meal from the mouth to the anus. It explains how chewing and swallowing move food past the airway, how slow waves and enteric reflexes propel it, how the stomach makes acid, how gut hormones match secretion and motility to what reaches the duodenum, how carbohydrate, protein, and fat are digested and absorbed, and how defecation and vomiting are controlled. Board questions usually describe a meal, a receptor blocker, a nerve injury, or a set of electrolytes and ask you to predict the hormone, secretion, motor pattern, or acid-base change that follows. Each response is produced by a specific cell, nerve, or receptor, so knowing which one lets you predict the effect of losing it.
prerequisites: Layers of the gut wall and the positions of the myenteric and submucosal plexuses
Smooth muscle excitation-contraction coupling and gap junctions
G protein signaling (Gs, Gi, Gq, cAMP, IP3, and intracellular Ca2+)
Cranial nerves V, IX, X, and XII and the sacral spinal cord (S2 to S4)

connections.how: The monosaccharides and chylomicrons produced here are the substrates of glycolysis and of lipoprotein metabolism.
GIP and GLP-1 are incretins, so the gut shapes the insulin response to an oral meal.

connections.to: Neuroanatomy of the brainstem and sacral cord
connections.how: Swallowing and vomiting are medullary programs and defecation is a sacral reflex, so lesion level predicts the deficit.
The kidney decides whether the alkalosis of vomiting persists, through aldosterone, chloride, and potassium.
Achalasia, Hirschsprung disease, gastrinoma, and malabsorption are each the loss of one mechanism taught here.

terms.def: Pacemaker cells in the gut wall that generate slow waves and pass them to smooth muscle through gap junctions.
A rhythmic oscillation of smooth muscle membrane potential that sets the maximum frequency of contraction but does not by itself cause most contractions.
A Ca2+-carried action potential that fires on a slow wave crest when the membrane passes threshold and triggers contraction.
A cyclic fasting pattern of intense contractions that sweeps from the stomach to the ileum about every 90 to 120 minutes.
Vagally mediated relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter and proximal stomach that lets a swallowed bolus enter with little rise in pressure.
A combined response larger than the sum of the separate responses, as when histamine, acetylcholine, and gastrin act together on the parietal cell.
An epithelial cell that senses luminal contents and releases a hormone or paracrine signal from its basal surface.
A hydrolase anchored in the enterocyte microvillus membrane that completes digestion next to the transporters.
A small aggregate of bile salts, monoglycerides, fatty acids, cholesterol, and phospholipid that carries lipid through the unstirred water layer.
Enteric reflex in which rectal distension relaxes the internal anal sphincter.
Neurons of the area postrema, outside the blood-brain barrier, that detect emetic chemicals in blood and cerebrospinal fluid.

sections.title: Mastication, swallowing, and relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter

blocks.text: Mastication breaks food into small particles, mixes it with saliva, and enlarges the surface that digestive enzymes can reach. The four muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid, and lateral pterygoid) derive from the first pharyngeal arch and are all supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3). The masseter, temporalis, and medial pterygoid close the jaw, while the lateral pterygoids protrude the mandible and help open it; alternating action of the two sides produces the grinding movement. Rhythmic chewing is largely a brainstem reflex: a bolus pressing on the palate inhibits the jaw closers, the jaw drops, the stretch then triggers rebound contraction, and the cycle repeats while the cortex decides when it starts and stops.

Swallowing has three phases. The oral phase is voluntary: the tongue (CN XII) presses the bolus up against the hard palate and back into the oropharynx. Once the bolus stimulates receptors around the pharyngeal opening, afferents mainly in CN IX and CN X reach the swallowing center in the medulla and lower pons (around the nucleus tractus solitarius and nucleus ambiguus). From that point the pharyngeal and esophageal phases run as an involuntary reflex that cannot be stopped. The center drives a fixed motor sequence through CN V, IX, X, and XII and briefly inhibits the respiratory center, so breathing pauses while the airway is sealed.

blocks.title: The swallowing sequence
steps: Tongue pushes bolus into oropharynx (voluntary, CN XII)
Pharyngeal afferents (CN IX, X) activate medullary swallowing center
Soft palate rises and seals the nasopharynx
Larynx rises, epiglottis tilts, vocal folds close, breathing pauses
Upper esophageal sphincter (cricopharyngeus) relaxes
Pharyngeal constrictors drive bolus into the esophagus
Primary peristalsis carries bolus toward the stomach

blocks.caption: The oral phase is voluntary; every later step is a medullary reflex that protects the airway and clears the esophagus.

blocks.text: The upper third of the esophagus is skeletal muscle driven directly by vagal motor neurons of the nucleus ambiguus, the lower third is smooth muscle controlled by vagal preganglionic fibers acting through the myenteric plexus, and the middle third is mixed. The primary peristaltic wave continues the pharyngeal wave and reaches the stomach in about 8 to 10 seconds. If food remains, local distension starts secondary peristalsis through enteric and vagal reflexes without a new swallow.

The lower esophageal sphincter (LES) is tonically contracted circular smooth muscle that keeps gastric contents out of the esophagus. When a swallow begins, vagal preganglionic fibers activate inhibitory myenteric neurons that release nitric oxide and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP). Nitric oxide raises cGMP and VIP raises cAMP in the muscle; both lower cytosolic Ca2+, so the sphincter relaxes before the wave arrives. The same vagovagal pathway relaxes the fundus and upper body of the stomach (receptive relaxation), so a meal is accommodated with little rise in gastric pressure.

Acid in the esophagus, heartburn, and mucosal injury
Gastric pressure rises quickly with filling; early satiety
Medullary stroke or CN IX and X lesions
Pharyngeal phase and airway protection fail
blocks.caption: Each disorder removes one element of the sequence, and the symptom follows from that element.

sections.title: Slow waves, peristalsis, and the migrating motor complex

blocks.text: Gastrointestinal smooth muscle cells are linked by gap junctions, so each layer behaves as an electrical syncytium. Their membrane potential, normally about -50 to -60 mV, oscillates in slow waves of roughly 5 to 15 mV. Slow waves are generated by interstitial cells of Cajal (ICC), pacemaker cells concentrated at the myenteric plexus between the circular and longitudinal layers, and spread to the muscle through gap junctions.

In most regions a slow wave by itself does not cause contraction. Contraction needs spike potentials, which fire when a slow wave crest carries the membrane past threshold (about -40 mV) and which are carried mainly by Ca2+ entering through voltage-gated L-type channels. That Ca2+ triggers contraction. Because spikes occur only near crests, slow wave frequency sets the maximum contraction rate of each region, while nerves and hormones decide whether spikes occur and how many. Acetylcholine, stretch, and parasympathetic activity depolarize the muscle and increase spiking; norepinephrine hyperpolarizes it and reduces spiking.

blocks.title: Slow wave frequency by region
blocks.caption: The fall in frequency along the small intestine favors net aboral movement.

blocks.text: Peristalsis is a local reflex of the enteric nervous system, sometimes called the law of the gut. Distension stimulates mucosal enterochromaffin cells to release serotonin and activates intrinsic sensory neurons, which drive myenteric interneurons that send excitation orally and inhibition aborally. Above the bolus, excitatory motor neurons release acetylcholine and substance P and the circular muscle contracts; below it, inhibitory motor neurons release VIP and nitric oxide and the circular muscle relaxes. Because the circuit is intrinsic, peristalsis continues after vagotomy, but it fails wherever myenteric ganglia are missing.

blocks.title: The peristaltic reflex
steps: Bolus stretches the gut wall
Enterochromaffin cells release serotonin; intrinsic sensory neurons fire
Myenteric interneurons signal up and down the gut
Above bolus: ACh and substance P contract circular muscle
Below bolus: VIP and nitric oxide relax circular muscle
Bolus moves aborally and the reflex repeats
blocks.caption: Peristalsis needs only the myenteric plexus; extrinsic nerves adjust its strength.

blocks.text: Between meals the stomach and small intestine switch to the migrating motor complex (MMC), which recurs about every 90 to 120 minutes. Phase I is quiescence, phase II brings irregular contractions, and phase III is a few minutes of intense contractions at the maximal slow wave rate that moves from the stomach or duodenum to the ileum. The pylorus opens widely during phase III, so indigestible solids, debris, and bacteria are swept onward. Motilin from M cells of the duodenum and jejunum rises cyclically during fasting and initiates gastric phase III. Eating suppresses motilin and replaces the MMC with mixing contractions. Erythromycin binds motilin receptors, which is why it provokes strong gastric contractions.

Loss of the MMC, as in diabetic autonomic neuropathy or systemic sclerosis, lets bacteria accumulate in the small intestine (small intestinal bacterial overgrowth). In Hirschsprung disease, neural crest cells fail to colonize the rectum and a variable length of distal colon, so the aganglionic segment has no inhibitory neurons, stays contracted, and obstructs the dilated bowel above it.

blocks.predict: After a truncal vagotomy, does peristalsis in the small intestine continue?
blocks.explain: Yes. The peristaltic reflex is built from intrinsic sensory neurons, interneurons, and motor neurons within the myenteric plexus. Vagotomy weakens extrinsic modulation and abolishes receptive relaxation of the stomach, but the local circuit still contracts above and relaxes below a bolus. Peristalsis fails only where the plexus itself is absent, as in Hirschsprung disease.

sections.title: Gastric acid secretion and its regulation

blocks.text: Parietal (oxyntic) cells in the glands of the gastric body and fundus secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor. Inside the cell, carbonic anhydrase converts CO2 and water to H+ and HCO3-. The H+/K+ ATPase pumps H+ into the lumen in exchange for K+, while HCO3- leaves across the basolateral membrane in exchange for Cl-, producing the alkaline tide in gastric venous blood after a meal. Cl- and K+ leave through apical channels, so K+ recycles and HCl accumulates. At rest the pumps sit in cytoplasmic tubulovesicles; stimulation inserts them into the apical canalicular membrane, making the pump the final common step for every stimulus.

blocks.title: Regulators of the parietal cell
rows: Stimulates parietal cells and ECL cells
Stimulates parietal cells weakly and ECL histamine release strongly
Strong stimulation; potentiates the other two
D cells of the antrum and body
Inhibits parietal, G, and ECL cells
blocks.caption: Three stimulants converge on one pump; somatostatin opposes all three.

blocks.text: Histamine signals through cAMP while acetylcholine and gastrin signal through Ca2+, so together they produce more acid than the sum of their separate effects (potentiation). Much of gastrin's action is indirect, through ECL histamine. Potentiation explains why an H2 receptor antagonist also reduces acid secreted in response to acetylcholine and gastrin, whereas blocking the H+/K+ ATPase stops acid whatever the stimulus.

Antral D cells sense luminal acid. When antral pH falls below about 3, they release somatostatin, which inhibits gastrin release and acid secretion once the meal's buffering capacity is used up. The vagus pushes the other way: it stimulates G cells through gastrin-releasing peptide (GRP) and inhibits D cells. Because the G cell transmitter is GRP rather than acetylcholine, atropine does not block vagally driven gastrin release.

blocks.title: Somatostatin feedback on acid secretion
steps: Food buffers acid and antral pH rises
G cells release gastrin
ECL histamine and parietal cells increase HCl
Antral pH falls below about 3
D cells release somatostatin
Gastrin and acid secretion fall
blocks.caption: Negative feedback through antral pH limits acid output once buffering is exhausted.

blocks.title: Phases of gastric acid secretion
rows: Sight, smell, taste, chewing, thought of food
Vagus: ACh to parietal and ECL cells, GRP to G cells
Distension; peptides and amino acids in the stomach
Protein products in the duodenum stimulate slightly; acid, fat, and hyperosmolar chyme inhibit
Duodenal gastrin; inhibition by secretin, GIP, and the enterogastric reflex
blocks.caption: Each phase is named for where the signal starts; the intestinal phase is mainly inhibitory.

blocks.text: Feedback explains two opposite causes of high gastrin. A gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome) secretes gastrin autonomously, so acid stays high despite low pH; the result is multiple or distal duodenal and jejunal ulcers, and diarrhea with steatorrhea because acid inactivates pancreatic lipase and precipitates bile salts. In autoimmune atrophic gastritis, parietal cells are destroyed, acid is absent, D cells are no longer stimulated, and gastrin rises steeply, which also drives ECL cell hyperplasia.

blocks.predict: How does fasting serum gastrin change when parietal cell acid secretion is suppressed for months?
blocks.explain: It rises. Without acid, antral pH stays high, D cells release little somatostatin, and G cells are released from inhibition. The same feedback explains the very high gastrin of atrophic gastritis, whereas in gastrinoma the gastrin is high while acid is also high.
blocks.check: The somatostatin feedback cycle and the final paragraph.

sections.title: Gut hormones and the response to a meal

blocks.text: Enteroendocrine cells are scattered among the epithelial cells of the stomach and small intestine. Their apical surfaces sample the lumen, and their basal granules release hormone into the blood when they detect a particular nutrient, acid, stretch, or neural signal. Each hormone therefore reports one feature of the chyme, and its actions correct that feature: secretin answers acid, CCK answers fat and protein, and GIP answers absorbed fuel.

blocks.title: The five classic gut hormones
rows: Peptides and amino acids, gastric distension, vagal GRP; inhibited by antral pH below about 3
Gastric acid secretion (directly and through ECL histamine), growth of the gastric mucosa
Fatty acids, monoglycerides, amino acids, and small peptides
Pancreatic enzyme secretion, gallbladder contraction, sphincter of Oddi relaxation, slower gastric emptying, satiety
Duodenal pH below about 4.5; fatty acids
Pancreatic and biliary HCO3- secretion; inhibits gastrin and gastric acid
Insulin release when glucose is high (incretin); reduces gastric acid at high levels
Fasting, released in cycles; suppressed by eating
Initiates phase III of the migrating motor complex
blocks.caption: Source cell letters: G for gastrin, I for CCK, S for secretin, K for GIP, M for motilin.

blocks.text: The hormones fall into structural families. Gastrin and CCK share the same five C-terminal amino acids. The CCK-B receptor binds both about equally, which is how gastrin acts on parietal and ECL cells, whereas the CCK-A receptor, which mediates gallbladder contraction and pancreatic secretion, strongly prefers CCK. Secretin, GIP, VIP, and glucagon form a second family.

Secretin acts on pancreatic duct cells through cAMP, opening CFTR Cl- channels; luminal Cl- then exchanges for HCO3-, which pours into the duct. The response is proportional to the acid load because secretin release continues until duodenal pH rises. CCK stimulates acinar enzyme secretion, partly through vagovagal reflexes, and CCK and secretin potentiate each other on the pancreas. GIP explains why oral glucose releases more insulin than the same glucose given intravenously: GIP and GLP-1 (from L cells) amplify insulin release only when glucose is high.

blocks.title: Predicting the response to an acidic, fatty meal
blocks.text: Acidic chyme rich in fat enters the duodenum. First, duodenal pH below about 4.5 stimulates S cells: secretin rises, pancreatic and biliary bicarbonate neutralize the acid, and secretin inhibits gastrin. Second, fatty acids and monoglycerides stimulate I cells: CCK rises, enzymes are secreted, the gallbladder contracts, the sphincter of Oddi relaxes, and gastric emptying slows. Third, fatty acids and any glucose stimulate K cells: GIP rises and enhances insulin release. Fourth, gastrin and acid fall, because secretin inhibits G cells, antral acid releases somatostatin, and the enterogastric reflex adds neural inhibition. Fifth, feeding suppresses motilin, so the MMC stops. Net effect: the duodenum slows delivery from the stomach and neutralizes and digests what has already arrived.

Measured hormone levels follow from the same logic. Excess gastrin with high acid points to a gastrinoma; in that tumor, intravenous secretin paradoxically raises gastrin, the reverse of its effect on normal G cells. Loss of duodenal mucosa in celiac disease reduces secretin and CCK release, which weakens pancreatic and gallbladder responses and adds to malabsorption.

sections.title: Digestion and absorption of carbohydrate, protein, and fat

blocks.text: Dietary starch is amylose (straight alpha 1,4 glucose chains) and amylopectin (alpha 1,4 chains with alpha 1,6 branches). Salivary alpha-amylase starts digestion but is inactivated by gastric acid once it mixes with chyme, so pancreatic alpha-amylase does most of the work in the duodenum. Amylase cleaves only internal alpha 1,4 bonds, leaving maltose, maltotriose, and alpha-limit dextrins that retain the branch points; it cannot cleave the beta 1,4 bonds of cellulose, so fiber reaches the colon intact. Brush border enzymes finish the job next to the transporters: lactase splits lactose, sucrase-isomaltase splits sucrose and the alpha 1,6 bonds of limit dextrins, and maltase-glucoamylase splits maltose and maltotriose. Glucose and galactose enter by SGLT1, which couples them to two Na+ ions using the gradient made by the basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase; fructose enters by facilitated diffusion through GLUT5; all three leave through GLUT2.

Protein digestion begins with pepsin, formed from chief cell pepsinogen in acid and active at pH about 2 to 3, but it is not essential. The decisive step is in the duodenum: enteropeptidase (enterokinase), anchored in the brush border, converts trypsinogen to trypsin. Trypsin then activates more trypsinogen and the other zymogens: chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, procarboxypeptidases, prophospholipase A2, and procolipase. Keeping the activator on the intestinal surface, along with storage as zymogens and trypsin inhibitor (SPINK1) in acinar cells, protects the pancreas from digesting itself; premature trypsin activation underlies pancreatitis. Brush border peptidases produce amino acids and di- and tripeptides. Peptides enter by the H+-coupled transporter PepT1 and amino acids by Na+-dependent carriers, and cytoplasmic peptidases release amino acids to the portal blood.

Fat is mostly triglyceride, and the problem is that lipase works only at an oil-water interface. Gastric churning and bile salts, which are amphipathic, emulsify fat into small droplets. Bile salts on the droplet surface would displace pancreatic lipase, so colipase anchors lipase to the surface. Lipase removes the fatty acids at positions 1 and 3, leaving 2-monoglyceride; cholesterol esterase and phospholipase A2 digest the other lipids. Long-chain fatty acids reach the blood by lymph, while medium-chain fatty acids enter portal blood directly.

blocks.text: The rectum is usually empty until a mass movement, a strong propulsive contraction of a long colonic segment that occurs a few times a day, pushes feces into it. Two sphincters keep the anal canal closed. The internal anal sphincter is a thickening of the circular smooth muscle; it is tonically contracted, provides most of the resting anal pressure, and is not under voluntary control. The external anal sphincter is skeletal muscle supplied by the inferior rectal branches of the pudendal nerve (S2 to S4); together with the puborectalis sling, which holds the anorectal angle, it is under voluntary control.

Rectal distension starts two reflexes. The intrinsic myenteric reflex sends peristaltic waves through the descending and sigmoid colon and relaxes the internal sphincter (the rectoanal inhibitory reflex), but it is weak alone. A parasympathetic reflex through the sacral cord amplifies it: afferents enter the cord and pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2 to S4) return to strengthen colonic contraction and internal sphincter relaxation. At the same time the sensation of rectal filling reaches the cortex.

blocks.title: The defecation reflex
steps: Mass movement fills and stretches the rectum
Myenteric reflex relaxes internal sphincter; urge is felt
Sacral parasympathetic reflex (pelvic nerves, S2 to S4) amplifies contraction
Cortex chooses: keep external sphincter closed or relax it
If delayed, rectum accommodates and urge fades
If allowed, puborectalis relaxes and Valsalva expels stool
blocks.caption: The internal sphincter relaxes by reflex; the decision is made at the external sphincter.

blocks.text: If the time is not right, voluntary contraction of the external sphincter and puborectalis holds stool back; the rectal wall relaxes to accommodate the volume, the internal sphincter regains tone, and the urge fades until the next mass movement. When defecation is chosen, both skeletal muscles relax, the anorectal angle straightens, and a Valsalva maneuver raises intra-abdominal pressure.

In the gastrocolic reflex, distension of the stomach after a meal increases colonic motility and mass movements within minutes, through extrinsic autonomic nerves and enteric pathways, with gastrin and CCK possibly contributing. It explains the urge to defecate soon after eating, especially after breakfast.

blocks.predict: After a pudendal nerve stretch injury in childbirth, will the internal sphincter still relax when the rectum fills, and what symptom follows?
blocks.explain: Yes. The rectoanal inhibitory reflex is enteric and the amplifying reflex uses pelvic splanchnic nerves, not the pudendal nerve. The internal sphincter therefore relaxes normally, but the weakened external sphincter cannot hold stool back, so she has urge incontinence.

sections.title: Vomiting and the metabolic alkalosis it causes

blocks.text: Vomiting is a coordinated motor program that empties the upper gut. It is organized by the vomiting center, a network in the dorsal medulla centered on the nucleus tractus solitarius and adjacent reticular formation rather than a single nucleus. The chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ) lies in the area postrema in the caudal floor of the fourth ventricle. Its fenestrated capillaries leave it outside the blood-brain barrier, so it detects drugs, toxins, and uremic solutes that most neurons cannot reach and relays them to the vomiting center.

rows: Area postrema to nucleus tractus solitarius
Vagal afferents; serotonin from enterochromaffin cells
blocks.caption: Blood-borne emetics act at the CTZ, gut irritants mainly through vagal 5-HT3 afferents.

blocks.title: The act of vomiting
steps: Nausea with salivation, sweating, pallor, and tachycardia
Retrograde contraction returns small bowel contents to stomach
Deep inspiration; glottis closes; soft palate seals nasopharynx

blocks.caption: Airway protection mirrors swallowing; the force comes from abdominal and diaphragmatic muscle, not the stomach.

blocks.text: For every H+ the parietal cell secretes, one HCO3- enters the blood. Normally that bicarbonate is matched when acid entering the duodenum triggers secretin and pancreatic HCO3- secretion. When gastric HCl is vomited, the pancreas is not stimulated, the bicarbonate stays in the plasma, and Cl- is lost: this generates a hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. Gastric fluid contains little K+ (roughly 5 to 10 mEq/L), so the vomitus accounts for only a small part of the K+ deficit.

A healthy kidney would excrete the extra bicarbonate quickly; vomiting maintains the alkalosis through three changes. Volume depletion activates renin, angiotensin II, and aldosterone. Angiotensin II increases proximal HCO3- reabsorption through the Na+/H+ exchanger, and aldosterone increases Na+ reabsorption by principal cells, making the lumen more negative and increasing K+ secretion by principal cells and H+ secretion by alpha-intercalated cells. Chloride depletion limits bicarbonate secretion by the pendrin Cl-/HCO3- exchanger of beta-intercalated cells. Hypokalemia shifts H+ into cells and increases H+ secretion and ammoniagenesis. The resulting urine Cl- is low, often below about 20 mEq/L, and late in the course the urine can be paradoxically acidic. Respiratory compensation by hypoventilation raises PaCO2 by about 0.7 mmHg for each 1 mEq/L rise in HCO3-. Restoring volume and chloride removes the stimulus, so this alkalosis is called saline-responsive.

blocks.title: Generation and maintenance of the alkalosis
steps: Vomiting removes HCl from the stomach
Retained HCO3- raises pH; plasma Cl- falls
Volume loss activates renin, angiotensin II, and aldosterone
Aldosterone increases urinary K+ and H+ loss
Hypokalemia and low Cl- sustain HCO3- reabsorption
Alkalosis persists until volume and Cl- are restored
blocks.caption: Loss of acid starts the alkalosis; the kidney's response to volume and chloride loss keeps it going.

blocks.title: Reading the electrolytes after prolonged vomiting
blocks.text: After four days of vomiting: Na+ 132, K+ 2.9, Cl- 86, HCO3- 34 mEq/L, arterial pH 7.48, PaCO2 47 mmHg, urine Cl- 8 mEq/L. pH above 7.45 with HCO3- above 26 mEq/L is metabolic alkalosis. Expected PaCO2 is 40 + 0.7 x (34 - 24), or 47 mmHg, so compensation is appropriate. The anion gap is 132 - (86 + 34) = 12 mEq/L, normal. Low plasma and urine Cl- mark chloride and volume loss, a saline-responsive pattern; mineralocorticoid excess would give high urine Cl-. The low K+ reflects renal wasting driven by aldosterone. Diarrhea gives the opposite: bicarbonate loss and a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis.

integration.text: Anatomy and embryology set the wiring. Chewing and swallowing depend on first arch muscles and the brainstem nuclei of CN V, IX, X, and XII, so a medullary stroke impairs swallowing while sparing the intrinsic motility of the stomach and intestine. Neural crest cells form the enteric plexuses, so their failure to migrate (Hirschsprung disease) or their destruction (achalasia, Chagas disease) removes inhibitory neurons and leaves smooth muscle unable to relax. Defecation depends on the sacral cord, so the level of a spinal lesion predicts reflex or areflexic bowel function.

Physiology, biochemistry, and pathology then explain the outputs. G protein messengers explain potentiation at the parietal cell, and negative feedback through somatostatin explains why gastrin is high both in gastrinoma and in atrophic gastritis. Enzyme biochemistry explains which nutrient fails first in each malabsorption, and lipoprotein assembly links fat absorption to chylomicron metabolism. Renal physiology decides whether vomiting produces a lasting alkalosis. The limits are that many values here (slow wave rates, phase percentages, pH thresholds) are approximate, and that hormone actions overlap, so board questions test the dominant effect rather than every effect.

summary: All muscles of mastication are supplied by CN V3; the oral phase of swallowing is voluntary, and the pharyngeal and esophageal phases are a medullary reflex that protects the airway.
Vagal inhibitory neurons release nitric oxide and VIP to relax the LES and proximal stomach; their loss causes achalasia.
Interstitial cells of Cajal set slow wave frequency (about 3 per minute in the stomach, 12 in the duodenum); contraction needs Ca2+ spike potentials on the crests.
Peristalsis is a myenteric reflex: ACh and substance P contract above the bolus, VIP and nitric oxide relax below it.
Motilin drives the fasting MMC about every 90 to 120 minutes; feeding stops it, and its loss favors bacterial overgrowth.

ACh (M3, Ca2+), gastrin (CCK-B, Ca2+, mostly via ECL histamine), and histamine (H2, cAMP) potentiate one another at the parietal cell; the H+/K+ ATPase is the final step and somatostatin is the brake.
Acid and fat in the duodenum raise secretin, CCK, and GIP, lower gastrin, acid, and motilin, and slow gastric emptying.
Enteropeptidase activates trypsinogen, trypsin activates the other zymogens, and lipase needs colipase and bile salt micelles; chylomicrons leave through lacteals.

Rectal distension relaxes the internal sphincter by reflex; the pudendal nerve gives voluntary control of the external sphincter, so internal sphincter loss causes passive leakage and external sphincter loss causes urge incontinence.

Prolonged vomiting causes hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, generated by HCl loss and maintained by volume depletion, aldosterone, hypokalemia, and chloride depletion, with low urine Cl-.

verify: Slow wave frequencies (about 3 per minute in the stomach, 12 in the duodenum, 8 to 9 in the terminal ileum) and the spike threshold of about -40 mV follow Guyton and Hall; other texts give slightly different values.
The 30%, 60%, and 10% split among cephalic, gastric, and intestinal phases is the Guyton and Hall estimate; some sources give different proportions.
MMC cycle length is quoted from about 90 to 120 minutes in different texts; confirm the value NABNE expects.
The antral pH threshold for somatostatin release (about 3) and the duodenal pH threshold for secretin release (about 4.5) are approximate consensus values.
Gastric fluid K+ concentration (roughly 5 to 10 mEq/L) and the urine Cl- cutoff for saline-responsive alkalosis (below about 20 mEq/L; some sources use 10 or 25) vary between references.
The compensation estimate for metabolic alkalosis (PaCO2 rises about 0.7 mmHg per 1 mEq/L rise in HCO3-) is a common rule; other formulas give similar but not identical values.
